title: As light belongs to the sun
hook: Ravana offers Sita his kingdom, and she answers through a blade of grass
carry: sita and ram, never apart, like light and sun

segments.voice: Yesterday: ashoka, the grove called without sorrow, and Sita in it. Your line: the light within is covered, never put out.
screen: `THE LIGHT WITHIN IS COVERED, NEVER PUT OUT.`

segments.voice: Hanuman is still hidden in the tree, working out how to approach Sita, when the garden fills with light and noise. Night is ending. Torches. Music. Ravana is coming, surrounded by his queens, walking straight toward the woman Hanuman just found. Hanuman makes himself even smaller in the leaves and holds perfectly still. And Sita, seeing who it is, pulls her knees up and wraps her arms around herself.
screen: `TORCHES BEFORE DAWN.` → `RAVANA COMES TO THE GROVE.` → `SITA DRAWS IN.`

segments.voice: Ravana speaks first, a long, smooth speech. He praises her beauty. He offers her everything: his kingdom, his wealth, the place of chief queen above all his wives. Forget Rama, he says, a beggar in the forest; you'll never see him again. Before Sita answers, she places a blade of grass between herself and him. In Sanskrit, tṛṇam antarataḥ kṛtvā: putting a blade of grass in between. Readers take it several ways: that she won't face him directly, that he's worth no more to her than grass, that even grass is a wall he cannot cross. Valmiki doesn't explain; he lets her do it. Then her words: I am no more apart from Rama than light is from the sun. Give me back to him, if you want to live. Ravana gives her two months, then storms off, and Hanuman, hidden in the branches, has heard every word. Hold on to her image, because Hindus never let it go. Light isn't added to the sun; it is the sun, shining. That's how the tradition sees Sita and Rama: not a hero and his prize, but one divine pair, so close you can't say one name without the other. It's why people chant Sita-Ram as if it were one word, and why so many greet each other with Jai Siya Ram, Sita's name first. Many teachers go further and call Sita Rama's own shakti, his power: the light of the sun itself.
screen: `RAVANA OFFERS EVERYTHING.` · `A BLADE OF GRASS BETWEEN THEM.` · `LIGHT AND SUN, NEVER APART.` · then, large: `SITA-RAM, ONE NAME.`

segments.voice: If you pray, chant Sita Ram softly, the way many Hindus do: Sita on the in-breath, Ram on the out-breath, for a few quiet rounds. If you don't pray, picture sunlight falling on a wall, and notice you can't have the light without the sun. Then bring to mind one bond in your own life you'd never trade, however sweetly it's asked for, and let the breath hold it steady.
The ashoka grove. Where Ravana offers Sita his kingdom, and she answers through a blade of grass: she is no more apart from Rama than light is from the sun.
Your line: Sita and Ram, never apart, like light and sun. That's why Jai Siya Ram says her name first. Rest well.

fork.reveal: Sita told Ravana she was no more apart from Rama than light is from the sun. Hindus keep the pair in one name, often with Sita's first.

original.note: Sanskrit ananyā, 'not other': Sita's word for herself in her reply, not apart from Rama, as light is not apart from the sun.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sita in captivity is simply helpless, waiting to be rescued.
what it means: she refuses Ravana and names herself one with Rama, as light is one with the sun; Hindus still say their names as one.

what a scholar hears: Sita's word is ananyā, 'not other'; devotional traditions read the pair as God and his shakti, and the blade of grass (tṛṇam antarataḥ kṛtvā) is read as distance, contempt or a boundary.
recall: the monkey king, Rama's sworn friend
